summary: This standards-track RFC defines Alternative Services for HTTP. They let an origin's resources be authoritatively available at a different network location, possibly reached with a different protocol configuration.

eli5.summary: A shop telling you it has another door, maybe a faster one, that still leads to the same store.

questions: how do i advertise http/3 support
what does the alt-svc header do
what does http 421 misdirected request mean
subtitle: How a web server can say 'you can also reach me over there', with a different host, port or protocol.

tldr.problem: HTTP URIs both name and locate a resource, so a server cannot easily point clients to another network location or protocol for the same origin without changing the identifier.
tldr.mechanism: An origin advertises alternative services (a protocol, host and port) using the Alt-Svc header field or the HTTP/2 ALTSVC frame, with a freshness lifetime. Clients that can verify the alternative is valid for the origin may use it.
tldr.outcome: Clients keep the same URI, Host and security context while connecting elsewhere. They can signal this with Alt-Used, and a 421 response tells them to drop an alternative that is not authoritative.

today: RFC 7838 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2016. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Separating Name from Location
sections.content:
HTTP conflates identifying a resource with locating it: http:// and https:// URIs both name and find things. Sometimes it is useful to keep the identifier but interact at a different network location.

The RFC lists examples. An origin server might redirect clients to a different server when it is under load or a more local one exists. It might offer a new protocol such as HTTP/2, or one with improved security such as TLS. Or it might segment clients by capability, such as support for Server Name Indication (SNI).

The RFC introduces Alternative Services as a general framework, two ways to advertise them (the Alt-Svc header field and the HTTP/2 ALTSVC frame), the Alt-Used request header, and an endorsement of status code 421 (Misdirected Request).
sections.eli5: A web address says what you want, not exactly where to get it. This RFC lets a site say, 'same thing, other door.'

sections.title: Alternative Service Concepts
sections.content:
An origin that can be reached through a different protocol, host and port combination has an alternative service. For example, the origin ("http", "www.example.com", "80") might declare ("h2", "new.example.com", "81"). An alternative service is identified by an ALPN protocol name, a host and a port, and each one MUST have a freshness lifetime in seconds. Alternatives apply to a whole origin, not to selected resources.

Alternatives are like extra routing information, comparable to DNS CNAME or SRV records. Clients MUST NOT let the change leak to the application: the URI, scheme, host and port stay the same, and the Host header is still derived from the origin. When TLS is used, the alternative must present a certificate for the origin's host name, not its own. Debugging tools MAY show the change.

Using alternatives is optional for clients. If one is fresh and its security is at least as desirable as the existing connection, a client SHOULD use it for all requests to that origin.
sections.eli5: You still walk into the same shop and ask for things by the same name. Only the street door you used is different.

sections.title: Trust, Caching and Use
sections.content:
Clients MUST have reasonable assurances that the alternative is under control of and valid for the whole origin. A TLS-based protocol with the certificate checks from RFC 2818 meets that bar. So an h2 alternative whose certificate is valid for the origin's host can be used, but an h2c alternative cannot, because that protocol has no way to establish the relationship. A client MUST NOT use a TLS-based alternative unless it supports SNI, and the SNI value is that of the origin.

Caching is governed by the freshness lifetime. Existing connections may continue after it expires; it limits only new connections. When a client detects a network change, it SHOULD drop cached alternatives that lack the persist flag with the value 1.

A client configured to use a proxy SHOULD NOT connect directly to an alternative but route through the proxy. If the connection fails, the client MAY fall back to the origin or another alternative, though this could be a downgrade attack. If the expected protocol is not negotiated, the connection MUST be considered failed.
sections.eli5: Before using the second door, you check that the shop really owns it. If the door turns out to be wrong, you go back to the main entrance.

sections.title: The Alt-Svc Header Field
sections.content:
An origin server can add an Alt-Svc header field to any response, regardless of status code. The value is either the keyword clear, which invalidates all cached alternatives for that origin, or a list of alternatives. Each alternative is a protocol-id (the percent-encoded ALPN name), an equals sign and a quoted alt-authority of the form [host]:port. Examples: Alt-Svc: h2=":8000" (same host, port 8000) and Alt-Svc: h2="new.example.org:80" (different host). When several are listed, the order shows the server's preference.

Parameters follow after semicolons. Two are defined, and unknown parameters MUST be ignored. ma is the max age in seconds; without it an alternative is fresh for 24 hours. persist=1 hints that it remains useful after a network change; other values MUST be ignored. For example: Alt-Svc: h2=":443"; ma=2592000; persist=1.

A received Alt-Svc value invalidates and replaces all cached alternatives for that origin. The HTTP cache lifetime does not affect it. Servers using HTTP/2 SHOULD send an ALTSVC frame instead, although the header remains valid there.
sections.eli5: The server writes a short note on its reply: 'also try door h2 at this address, and remember it for this long.' A newer note replaces the old one.

sections.title: ALTSVC Frame, Alt-Used and 421
sections.content:
The ALTSVC frame (type 0xa, decimal 10) advertises an alternative to an HTTP/2 client. It is a non-critical extension, so endpoints that do not know it ignore it. The payload holds a 16-bit Origin-Len, an optional Origin and the Alt-Svc field value. On a stream other than 0 it applies to that stream's origin, and Origin MUST be empty. On stream 0 the Origin field MUST be present and anything the client does not consider authoritative MUST be ignored. A server MUST ignore the frame, and an intermediary MUST NOT forward it. It acts like receiving an Alt-Svc header, replacing cached alternatives.

Clients using an alternative SHOULD send an Alt-Used header in all requests, such as Alt-Used: alternate.example.net. It lets alternatives detect loops and balance load.

Status code 421 (Misdirected Request) from an alternative means it is not authoritative. The client MUST remove that origin's cache entry and MAY retry at another alternative or the origin. An Alt-Svc header in a 421 response MUST be ignored.
sections.eli5: Some servers can also shout the news through a special loudspeaker message. Clients show which door they used, and a 'wrong door' answer means they should forget that door.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Changing ports is risky: an attacker who can inject Alt-Svc and listen on the advertised port can hijack an origin, for instance on shared servers where users control pages. Changing hosts lets an attacker masquerade as the origin, and a large freshness lifetime could persist a man-in-the-middle attack. The host authentication in section 2.1 mitigates these, and certificate-pinning checks MUST be applied to alternatives as for direct connections.

Changing protocols may weaken security, so clients cannot use alternatives blindly. Unique alternative host names could be used to track clients, especially with persist, and user agents MUST remove alternative service information when origin data such as cookies is cleared. Servers should not infer security from port 443; they should use the scheme the protocol carries, or avoid advertising alternatives for insecure schemes.
sections.eli5: A fake door could trick you into giving secrets to the wrong place, so you check IDs, forget doors when asked, and do not assume a door is safe just because of its number.

data.title: Alt-Svc header field values
data.code:
Alt-Svc: h2=":8000"
Alt-Svc: h2="new.example.org:80"
Alt-Svc: h2="alt.example.com:8000", h2=":443"
Alt-Svc: h2=":443"; ma=2592000; persist=1
